Antarctica in a warming world

Antarctica in a Warming World plunges viewers into the heart of one of the planet’s most remote and fragile frontiers. Through compelling first-hand accounts from scientists, this short documentary reveals the concerning transformations unfolding across the continent and Southern Ocean.  Director Magnolia Lowe collaborated with Antarctic Science Platform researchers to share key findings from the past seven years of Aotearoa New Zealand’s Antarctic research, 2018 to 2025. The aim is to help people understand the current impacts of climate change, while also showcasing the breathtaking visuals of this unique region. Plain-language summaries distilling the research can be found at https://www.antarcticscienceplatform.org.nz/impactportfolio

Director: Magnolia Lowe
Production company: Magpie Content Creation
Directors of Photography: Jess Charlton (interviews) and Anthony Powell (Antarctica)
Underwater videography: Dr Leigh Tait
Additional videography: Lana Young

With special thanks to the Platform's New Zealand partners (2018-2025) Antarctica New Zealand, Cawthron Institute, Lincoln Agritech, 
Te Herenga Waka—Victoria University of Wellington, University of Auckland, University of Canterbury, University of Otago, The University of Waikato, Earth Sciences New Zealand (formerly GNS Science and NIWA), and the Bioeconomy Science Institute (formerly Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research).

Love these pictures? We do. Antarctica New Zealand helps content creators navigate access to a small but growing film library. For copyright, licensing and crediting info, please contact c.team@antarcticanz.govt.nz

City Rail Link- the construction of Beresford Square 2020-2025

The fences finally down  recently— and Beresford Square opened to the public for the first time since 2020. A massive milestone.

Native trees softening the edges behind the service building
Beautiful te ao Māori artwork woven into the design
A new retail space ready to open alongside CRL next year.

It’s already buzzing as a proper community space — a spot to meet, relax, wander, and soak in the new energy around Karanga-a-Hape Station which opens in 2026.
And like every big construction win, this one has a story.
Here’s a time-lapse capturing the journey from boots-on-the-ground to the vibrant square you can step into today.

Limited title surveys webinar: Introduction to updated guidance

Join us for an introduction to LINZ's updated guidance on surveys to remove limitations. 

We'll cover the basics and what's changed, including when: 
- long-standing occupation can take precedence over title dimensions to define the extent of the land in the title 
- a boundary defined on a prior removal of limitations survey can be used to define the common boundary with the land under survey  
- new residue parcels can be created – only where occupation evidence supports a potential adverse possession claim  
- residue land from an adjoining cancelled limited title may be included in a removal of limitations survey without an adverse possession application.

This live webinar took place on 19 November 2025.

For more information on the updated guidance visit: https://www.linz.govt.nz/guidance/survey/cadastral-survey-guidelines/limited-title-surveys

Reversing Cultural Amnesia: Activating Māori Practice in Museums delivered by Dr Awhina Tamarapa

In 1947, Māori leader, politician, and scholar Apirana Ngata spoke to his scholarly peers at the Polynesian Society, announcing his greatest desire to revive Māori culture as a living force within communities, not be relegated to dead exhibits in museums (Ramsden 1948, 85).

This lecture acknowledges the concerns of visionary leaders and champions of cultural practice and their activation within museums. Through her work as a Māori curator, writer, cultural practitioner and post-doctoral researcher, Awhina Tamarapa advocates for cultural restoration as a form of liberation in a museum context. In her research, Tamarapa is exploring strategies for the recovery and reclamation of taonga puoro (singing treasures) and karetao (animated storytellers) for new generations.

There are challenges regarding taonga held by overseas museums. Concepts such as keeping taonga warm, and mana taonga, recognises the connection and authority of descendants to their taonga, that underpin this work.

The focus on the reclamation of Indigenous practice has been bolstered by working with First Nations, Canada BC. Led by Professor Bryony Onciul, University of Exeter, UK, Tamarapa was privileged to be part of a research project “The Future of Indigenous Rights and Responsibilities: Ancestral governance, environmental stewardship, language revival, and cultural vibrancy” funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council, UK.
